CohortHonestDiD: a detailed guide

Estimation, assumptions, options, and executed results

Ziyi Liu

Source: vignettes/detailed-guide.Rmd
detailed-guide.Rmd

Start here

This guide shows how to choose the assumptions, read the results, and use the main options of CohortHonestDiD 1.0.0, which implements Liu (2026), Cohort-Anchored HonestDiD. For a shorter introduction, see vignette("getting-started", package = "CohortHonestDiD"). For an applied analysis, read estimation, targets, and reading results. For estimates from other software, see external estimates; numerical controls explains computing costs and unresolved searches.

Write gg for a cohort’s adoption index on the ordered analysis grid, tt for a period index, and s=t−g+1s=t-g+1. Period s=1s=1 is the adoption period and s=0s=0 the last untreated period. Calendar labels are kept for display, but the restrictions use the ordered grid.

A cohort’s block bias Δg,s\Delta_{g,s} is its untreated-outcome trend relative to its initial control group under the estimator’s normalization: the units still untreated when it adopts for imp and cs_nyt, and the never-treated units for cs_nt. It enters the bias of the estimated coefficients through a known bias map, δ=WΔ\delta=W\Delta. The sensitivity restrictions apply to block biases; they place no restriction on how treatment effects change over time. The guide uses these terms:

  • Procedures. The conditional procedure (Conditional) and the conditional least-favorable hybrid (C-LF) of Andrews, Roth, and Pakes (2023) invert tests, so a confidence set can consist of several pieces. The fixed-length confidence interval (FLCI) of Armstrong and Kolesár (2018) is an optimized linear estimate plus or minus a half-length; it is available only under SD.
  • SD scope. The post-only restriction (full.path = FALSE) bounds the slope changes that involve post-treatment periods. The full-path restriction (full.path = TRUE) also bounds those among pre-treatment periods.
  • Plug-in identified set. The identified set computed as if the estimated coefficients were the true ones. ATT plots show it as a shaded band.
  • Framework. Cohort inference (framework = "cohort", the default) restricts each cohort’s block bias. Aggregate inference restricts the aggregated event-study coefficients instead. Both support ATT and dynamic targets; cohort-dynamic targets require the cohort framework.
Restriction Meaning of the bound Procedures Default procedure Default SD scope
Second differences (SD) Change in the slope of a cohort’s block-bias path between consecutive periods; outcome units FLCI, Conditional, C-LF C-LF Post-only (full path for FLCI)
Relative magnitudes (RM) Post-treatment change relative to the cohort’s largest pre-treatment change; no units Conditional, C-LF C-LF Not applicable

The paper recommends cohort inference with the Conditional or C-LF procedure, under the post-only restriction for SD; the defaults are cohort inference with C-LF, post-only under SD. cohort_fit(covariance = "CR2") gives the bias-reduced covariance (Section 2). Every interval in this guide is pointwise, not a simultaneous band over periods or bounds.

The sensitivity approach is that of Rambachan and Roth (2023), A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends, Review of Economic Studies, 90(5), 2555–2591, https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdad018. The data are the county minimum-wage application of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods, Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 200–230.

The code below uses three small helpers to print tables.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4.8, dpi = 120, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)
library(CohortHonestDiD)
library(ggplot2)
## Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.3
tab <- function(x, digits = 5, ...) knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, ...)
sets <- function(x) x$intervals[, c("target", "M", "component", "lower", "upper", "success", "status")]
rows <- function(xs, labels = names(xs)) do.call(rbind, Map(function(x, label) {
  cbind(example = label, sets(x))
}, xs, labels))

1. Fit the minimum-wage application

The bundled outcome Y is log teen employment. D equals one from the first year in which a county’s state minimum wage exceeds the federal minimum of $5.15, and treatment is absorbing.

data(minimum_wage)
tab(data.frame(rows = nrow(minimum_wage),
  counties = length(unique(minimum_wage$id)),
  first_year = min(minimum_wage$year), last_year = max(minimum_wage$year),
  periods = length(unique(minimum_wage$year))))
rows counties first_year last_year periods
15988 2284 2001 2007 7 
tab(head(minimum_wage[c("id", "year", "Y", "D")]))

8001 2002 8.54130 0

8001 2004 8.33687 0
8001 2005 8.34022 0
8001 2006 8.37816 0

Formula, column names, and estimator choice

The formula must be exactly outcome ~ treatment, with the unit and time columns in index, in that order. Covariates and transformations are not supported.

fit_imp <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                      estimator = "imp")
fit_nyt <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                      estimator = "cs_nyt")
fit_nt <- cohort_fit(data = minimum_wage, Y = "Y", D = "D", index = c("id", "year"),
                     estimator = "cs_nt")
print(fit_imp)
#> Cohort difference-in-differences fit
#> Estimator: imp 
#> Covariance: CR1 cluster-robust, 2284 clusters 
#> Cohorts: 3  | Coefficients: 21 
#>  cohort units clusters mass
#>       0  1377     1377 1377
#>       4   100      100  100
#>       6   223      223  223
#>       7   584      584  584

imp is the imputation estimator; cs_nyt and cs_nt are the Callaway-Sant’Anna estimators with not-yet-treated and never-treated controls. The column-name interface used for fit_nt is equivalent to the formula; supply one or the other.

empirical <- list(imp = fit_imp, cs_nyt = fit_nyt, cs_nt = fit_nt)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(empirical), function(nm) {
  x <- empirical[[nm]]
  j <- x$coordinate_info$type == "post"
  data.frame(estimator = nm, cohort = x$coordinate_info$cohort[j],
    relative_period = x$coordinate_info$relative_period[j],
    estimate = as.numeric(coef(x)[j]), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(x)))[j])
}))
tab(comparison)

The rows compare the same cohort-period cells; the estimators differ because they use different comparisons, in their control units and baseline periods. The full covariance includes dependence across periods and across cohorts.

The coefficient normalizations reduce the covariance rank by design, so compare the rank with normalized_dimension, and check the cluster and cell counts. With very few clusters, the estimated covariance can be unreliable even when the computation succeeds. plot(fit) shows conventional 95% pointwise intervals.

2. Weights, clusters, and panel histories

By default, the unit identifier defines the clusters and every unit has weight one. cluster and weights each accept a column name or a row-aligned vector. Both must be fixed within unit, so a time-varying population series cannot serve as weights; weights must also be positive and finite.

State clustering and fixed baseline weights

For illustration, the next fits cluster by state and weight each county by its baseline employment level. The rest of the guide is unweighted.

baseline <- minimum_wage[minimum_wage$year == min(minimum_wage$year), c("id", "Y")]
baseline$fixed_weight <- exp(baseline$Y) / mean(exp(baseline$Y))
weighted_data <- minimum_wage
weighted_data$fixed_weight <- baseline$fixed_weight[match(weighted_data$id, baseline$id)]
fit_state <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                        estimator = "cs_nt", cluster = "state")
#> Warning: Some cohorts or the never-treated group contain fewer than 10
#> clusters. Cluster covariance and sensitivity intervals may be unreliable;
#> inspect diagnostics$cohort_counts and diagnostics$cell_counts.
#> Warning: Some observed cohort-period cells contain only one cluster. Centered
#> covariance can collapse in directions supported by these cells.
fit_weighted <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = weighted_data, index = c("id", "year"),
                           estimator = "cs_nt", cluster = "state",
                           weights = "fixed_weight")
#> Warning: Some cohorts or the never-treated group contain fewer than 10
#> clusters. Cluster covariance and sensitivity intervals may be unreliable;
#> inspect diagnostics$cohort_counts and diagnostics$cell_counts.
#> Warning: Some observed cohort-period cells contain only one cluster. Centered
#> covariance can collapse in directions supported by these cells.
tab(data.frame(fit = c("unit clusters", "state clusters", "state clusters, fixed weights"),
  clusters = c(fit_nt$diagnostics$n_clusters, fit_state$diagnostics$n_clusters,
               fit_weighted$diagnostics$n_clusters)))
fit clusters
unit clusters 2284
state clusters 29
state clusters, fixed weights 29 
conventional_att <- function(x) {
  post <- x$coordinate_info$type == "post"
  w <- numeric(length(coef(x)))
  w[post] <- x$cohort_masses[as.character(x$coordinate_info$cohort[post])]
  w <- w / sum(w)
  c(estimate = sum(w * coef(x)), se = sqrt(drop(t(w) %*% vcov(x) %*% w)))
}
weighted_comparison <- t(vapply(list(unit_clusters = fit_nt,
  state_clusters = fit_state, state_clusters_fixed_weights = fit_weighted),
  conventional_att, c(estimate = 0, se = 0)))
tab(data.frame(fit = rownames(weighted_comparison), weighted_comparison))
fit estimate se
unit_clusters -0.05158 0.00665
state_clusters -0.05158 0.00961
state_clusters_fixed_weights -0.04482 0.01582

Changing the clusters changes the estimated uncertainty; changing the weights can also change the estimand and the estimates. The default covariance, covariance = "CR1", sums centered cohort-period scores within clusters and multiplies the sum of their outer products by G/(G−1)⋅(n−1)/(n−p)G/(G-1)\cdot(n-1)/(n-p), for GG clusters, nn usable rows, and pp nonempty cohort-period cells. The paper’s minimum-wage results use county clusters, as in the original study. Because minimum wages change at the state level, the paper’s appendix also reports state-clustered results without the 2004 cohort, which lies in a single state.

The bias-reduced CR2 covariance

covariance = "CR2" replaces the CR1 multiplier with the bias-reduced adjustment of Bell and McCaffrey (2002): each cluster’s score is divided by 1−pc\sqrt{1-p_c}, where pcp_c is the cluster’s share of the units of its cohort, measured by the unit weights when weights is supplied. Never-treated units form their own group. If a cluster contains units of several cohorts, the part of its score from each cohort is divided by 1−p\sqrt{1-p}, with pp its share of that cohort. The paper recommends CR2 with Conditional or C-LF inference when some cohorts contain only a few units or clusters. On unbalanced panels, CR2, like the bias map, is an approximation; ?cohort_fit gives the details.

fit_state_cr2 <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                            estimator = "cs_nt", cluster = "state", covariance = "CR2")
#> Warning: Some cohorts or the never-treated group contain fewer than 10
#> clusters. Cluster covariance and sensitivity intervals may be unreliable;
#> inspect diagnostics$cohort_counts and diagnostics$cell_counts.
#> Warning: Some observed cohort-period cells contain only one cluster. Centered
#> covariance can collapse in directions supported by these cells.
print(fit_state_cr2)
#> Cohort difference-in-differences fit
#> Estimator: cs_nt 
#> Covariance: CR2 bias-reduced cluster-robust, 29 clusters 
#> Cohorts: 3  | Coefficients: 21 
#>  cohort units clusters mass
#>       0  1377       16 1377
#>       4   100        1  100
#>       6   223        3  223
#>       7   584        9  584
shares <- fit_state_cr2$cluster_shares
tab(do.call(rbind, lapply(split(shares, shares$cohort), function(z)
  data.frame(cohort = z$cohort[1], clusters = nrow(z),
    largest_share = max(z$share), whole_cohort_clusters = sum(z$factor == 0)))))
cohort clusters largest_share whole_cohort_clusters
0 16 0.17865 0
4 1 1.00000 1
6 3 0.38117 0
7 9 0.19178 0 
tab(data.frame(covariance = c("CR1", "CR2"),
  rbind(conventional_att(fit_state), conventional_att(fit_state_cr2))))
covariance estimate se
CR1 -0.05158 0.00961
CR2 -0.05158 0.01040

A cluster that contains a whole cohort has a share of one. The part of its score from that cohort is zero under CR2, where its factor is zero, and, on a balanced panel, under CR1, where the cohort’s centered residuals cancel. That cohort’s sampling variation is then omitted. In these data, the 2004 cohort (adoption index 4 in the tables) lies in a single state with no other counties, and that state’s score is zero under both covariances. For every other cluster, the CR2 adjustment grows with its share.

A small panel for procedural examples

The next data are artificial: 72 units observed in four periods, of which 24 are never treated, 24 adopt in period 3, and 24 adopt in period 4. The last cohort has one post-treatment period and enough pre-treatment history. Later sections use this inexpensive design to illustrate procedures and options; its results are not findings.

set.seed(314159)
small <- expand.grid(id = seq_len(72), time = seq_len(4))
small$g <- rep(c(0, 3, 4), each = 24)[small$id]
small$D <- as.integer(small$g > 0 & small$time >= small$g)
small$Y <- 1 + small$id / 100 + .06 * small$time + .08 * small$D +
  rnorm(nrow(small), sd = .08)
small_fit <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = small, index = c("id", "time"), estimator = "imp")
tab(small_fit$diagnostics$cohort_counts)
cohort units clusters mass
0 24 24 24
3 24 24 24
4 24 24 24

Missing observations and treatment dating

Outcomes are never imputed. After a known treatment status, a missing status or an absent row is filled forward within unit; an unknown leading status stays unknown, and its outcome is excluded. Adoption is dated at the first observed treated status, so a missing stretch around adoption can hide the true date.

incomplete <- small[!(small$id == 1 & small$time == 2), ]
incomplete$Y[incomplete$id == 2 & incomplete$time == 3] <- NA
incomplete$D[incomplete$id == 25 & incomplete$time == 2] <- NA
incomplete$D[incomplete$id == 26 & incomplete$time == 1] <- NA
incomplete$D[incomplete$id == 27 & incomplete$time == 3] <- NA
incomplete_fit <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = incomplete, index = c("id", "time"),
                             estimator = "cs_nt")
#> Warning: Unbalanced sample: estimation uses observed outcomes and actual
#> available histories. W uses the balanced-panel formula with fixed cohort
#> masses; estimator equivalence and sensitivity-analysis coverage are not
#> guaranteed for this approximation.
missing_counts <- unlist(incomplete_fit$data_info$missingness)
tab(data.frame(diagnostic = names(missing_counts), value = unname(missing_counts)))

missing_outcomes_observed 1
treatment_filled 3
treatment_filled_observed_rows 2
treatment_filled_absent_rows 1
leading_unknown_treatment 1
outcomes_excluded_unknown_treatment 1
outcomes_imputed 0

  c("unit_id", "calendar_time", "Y", "D_original", "D", "observed_row",

The fit warns that the design is unbalanced. Estimation uses the observed histories, while W uses fixed cohort masses and the balanced mapping, so the paper’s balanced-panel coverage and equivalence results do not automatically apply. Check cell_counts before interpreting estimates: every required comparison must be estimable, and every included unit must have at least one usable outcome.

irregular <- small
irregular$time <- c(2001, 2002, 2004, 2007)[irregular$time]
irregular_fit <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = irregular, index = c("id", "time"),
                            estimator = "cs_nt")
#> Warning: Time labels are not equally spaced. Relative periods and curvature
#> bounds use the ordered observed time grid, not elapsed calendar time.
tab(data.frame(analysis_index = seq_along(irregular_fit$data_info$time_labels),
  calendar_label = irregular_fit$data_info$time_labels))
analysis_index calendar_label
1 2001
2 2002
3 2004
4 2007

Irregular numeric or date labels draw a warning and are treated as equally spaced analysis periods; character labels are used in sorted order. Treatment must be binary and absorbing, with a never-treated group and an observed untreated period for each treated unit. Units already treated at their first known status are not supported.

3. Targets and representations in the application

A target averages selected post-treatment cells. For selected cells JJ, a cell in cohort gg receives weight ℓj=mg/∑k∈Jmg(k)\ell_j=m_g/\sum_{k\in J}m_{g(k)}, where mgm_g is the cohort mass. The ATT selects all post-treatment cells, and earlier cohorts contribute more of them. A dynamic target selects one relative period, and a cohort-dynamic target selects one cell.

M_application <- c(0, .005, .01, .015, .02)
att <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                          target = "att", seed = 123)
dynamic <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = .015,
                              target = "dynamic", seed = 123)
cohort_dynamic <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = .015,
                                     target = "cohort-dynamic", seed = 123)
att_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                                    target = "att", framework = "aggregate", seed = 123)
dynamic_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = .015,
                                        target = "dynamic", framework = "aggregate",
                                        seed = 123)
tab(rows(list(cohort_ATT = att, aggregate_ATT = att_aggregate)))

SD bounds the second differences of each cohort’s block-bias path, |Δg,s−2Δg,s−1+Δg,s−2|≤M|\Delta_{g,s}-2\Delta_{g,s-1}+\Delta_{g,s-2}|\leq M, here in log-employment units. These calls use the defaults (C-LF, post-only). A larger M permits more curvature; the conventional estimate does not depend on M.

plot(att, main = "Cohort restrictions: minimum-wage ATT", ylab = "Log teen employment")

plot(att_aggregate, main = "Aggregate restrictions: minimum-wage ATT",
     ylab = "Log teen employment")

The dotted line is the conventional estimate, and the shaded band, drawn when its bounds are finite, is the plug-in identified set. Under the post-only restriction, the plug-in set is never empty, because the pre-treatment path is not restricted. The full-path restriction also bounds the curvature of the estimated pre-treatment paths. In this application those paths violate it at every displayed M, and the full-path plug-in sets are empty. The next chunk computes the full-path FLCI for comparison.

att_flci <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                               target = "att", method = "FLCI", seed = 123)
tab(data.frame(M = M_application,
  post_only_plugin_empty = vapply(att$results,
    function(z) isTRUE(z$diagnostics$plugin.empty), logical(1)),
  full_path_plugin_empty = vapply(att_flci$results,
    function(z) isTRUE(z$diagnostics$plugin.empty), logical(1))))
M post_only_plugin_empty full_path_plugin_empty

The plug-in calculation treats the estimated paths as fixed, whereas the FLCI accounts for sampling uncertainty and can be nonempty when the plug-in set is empty. An empty full-path plug-in set is therefore not by itself a specification test. The FLCI’s optimized center can differ from the conventional estimate.

Aggregate inference transforms the estimates and covariance to Aβ̂A\hat\beta and AΣA′A\Sigma A' and restricts the aggregated coefficients. The same numerical M therefore imposes a different assumption under cohort and aggregate inference.

On a balanced panel, appropriately normalized Imp and CS-NYT block biases differ only by cohort constants, which the SD and RM restrictions do not detect, so their cohort identified sets coincide. Because the package uses a common covariance construction and FLCI selection rule, the theoretical confidence sets coincide as well, under CR1 or CR2 (the CR2 shares do not depend on the estimator). Computed sets agree up to numerical precision when controls and seeds match, although either search can report an unresolved result. The equivalence does not cover conventional coefficients and standard errors, CS-NT, aggregate restrictions, covariances supplied to cohort_input(), or unbalanced panels. The comparison below uses the same bounds, seed, covariance, representation, and procedure.

att_nyt <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_nyt, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                              target = "att", seed = 123)
tab(data.frame(M = att$intervals$M, Imp_status = att$intervals$status,
  CS_NYT_status = att_nyt$intervals$status,
  lower_difference = att$intervals$lower - att_nyt$intervals$lower,
  upper_difference = att$intervals$upper - att_nyt$intervals$upper), digits = 10)

The weights show which cells define each estimand. Dynamic targets at different periods can average different cohorts, so changes across periods need not reflect a fixed cohort mix.

plot(dynamic, M = .015, main = "Dynamic effects at M = .015",
     ylab = "Log teen employment")

chosen_cohort <- sort(unique(fit_imp$coordinate_info$cohort))[1]
plot(cohort_dynamic, M = .015, cohorts = chosen_cohort,
     main = "One cohort: conventional estimates and sensitivity sets",
     ylab = "Log teen employment")

In plot(), M selects bounds that were already computed, and cohorts selects cohorts by adoption index; neither reruns inference.

Balanced targets and balanced aggregation

The balanced window contains the relative periods observed for every cohort. In this application it runs from s=−2s=-2, the first period of the 2004 cohort, to s=1s=1, because the 2007 cohort is treated for one year. With balanced = TRUE the ATT averages the window’s post-treatment cells with the same cohort weights in every period, here the effect in the first treated year. Aggregate inference then forms the aggregated event study only on the window, so the same cohorts enter every period.

M_balanced <- c(0, .01, .02)
att_balanced <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, M = M_balanced, balanced = TRUE, seed = 123)
att_balanced_window <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, M = M_balanced, balanced = TRUE,
                                          cohort.paths = "window", seed = 123)
att_balanced_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, M = M_balanced, balanced = TRUE,
                                             framework = "aggregate", seed = 123)
att_balanced$settings$window
#> lower upper 
#>    -2     1
tab(target_weights(att_balanced))

#>     att 0.02         1 -0.04013989 0.02949040     ok

Under cohort inference, cohort.paths = "full", the default, keeps each cohort’s whole path, as in the paper. cohort.paths = "window" uses each path only inside the window: the RM benchmark comes from the pre-treatment changes in the window, the full-path SD restriction bounds only the pre-treatment second differences in the window, and later periods are dropped. Under the post-only SD restriction used here, the two choices give the same plug-in identified set, and their confidence sets differ at most slightly. With one post-treatment period in the window, the post-only plug-in identified set is also the same under aggregate inference; the confidence sets differ because the two analyses use different coefficients and covariances.

Balanced aggregation changes the estimand. It removes the change in the cohorts averaged across periods, but not the change in the not-yet-treated comparison groups, which enters the imputation and CS-NYT biases through the bias map. In the paper’s simulations, aggregate inference on the balanced window comes closer to cohort inference but still differs from it. On a balanced panel, Imp and CS-NYT give the same balanced cohort inference under either cohort.paths value, but in general not the same aggregate inference. Balanced aggregate results store the aggregation matrix, the aggregated coefficients, and their covariance in aggregation.

FLCI weights

The FLCI is a linear estimator. Its weights on the post-treatment coefficients are the target weights, and flci_weights() tabulates the others: the weights vv on the pre-treatment coefficients (weights = "coefficients", the default) and the weights γ\gamma on the pure pre-treatment second differences ẑ\hat z (weights = "gamma"), with each weight’s contribution to the center. plot(result, type = "weights") draws them against the bound, one row per coefficient or second difference, grouped by cohort.

att_flci_post <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                                    target = "att", method = "FLCI",
                                    full.path = FALSE, seed = 123)
plot(att_flci_post, type = "weights", main = "Post-only FLCI: weights v")

plot(att_flci, type = "weights", main = "Full-path FLCI: weights v")

The post-only FLCI puts weight only on each cohort’s last two pre-treatment coefficients, s=−1s=-1 and s=0s=0: it subtracts the linear extrapolation of the cohort’s pre-treatment slope, and its weights do not depend on M. With CS-NYT it also weights the adjustment cohorts’ coefficients in the base period. The full-path FLCI adds D′γD'\gamma, a combination of the pure pre-treatment second differences, so its weights reach earlier periods. Each cohort’s pre-treatment coefficients satisfy one normalization (the imputation coefficients sum to zero, and the CS coefficient at s=0s=0 is zero), so the weights are unique only up to that direction. flci_weights() reports the paper’s form v=vP+D′γv=v^{P}+D'\gamma; results[[k]]$weights$coefficients stores its projection orthogonal to the normalization, which gives the same estimate.

plot(att_flci, type = "weights", weights = "gamma", labels = TRUE,
     main = "Full-path FLCI: weights gamma")

gamma_att <- flci_weights(att_flci, weights = "gamma")
centers <- attr(gamma_att, "centers")
tab(data.frame(M = centers$M, FLCI_center = centers$center,
  post_only_center = centers$post.only.center,
  sum_of_contributions = as.numeric(tapply(gamma_att$contribution, gamma_att$M, sum))))

At M=0M=0 the full-path FLCI uses every pure pre-treatment second difference as a control variate. Each unit of weight costs M of worst-case bias, so the weights shrink as M grows: at M = .005 and .01 only the 2004 cohort’s second difference keeps weight, and from M = .015 all weights are zero and the two FLCIs coincide. The contributions γjẑj\gamma_j\hat z_j add up to the FLCI center minus the post-only center, which is also the center of the post-only plug-in identified set. by = "cohort" sums them within each cohort. Imputation and CS-NYT give the same γ\gamma, centers, and contributions.

4. Procedures and SD scopes

The six comparisons below cross the three procedures with the two SD scopes. More pre-treatment periods give the full-path restriction more information about curvature. The comparisons use the artificial panel with 200 calibration draws and a 21-point grid to keep the guide quick. These are demonstration settings, not the defaults or a recommendation.

illustrative_control <- list(lf.sims = 200L, grid.points = 21L)
sd_examples <- list()
for (method in c("FLCI", "Conditional", "C-LF")) {
  for (full in c(FALSE, TRUE)) {
    label <- paste(method, if (full) "full path" else "post-only")
    sd_examples[[label]] <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "SD",
      M = c(0, .015), method = method, full.path = full, target = "att",
      seed = 2026, control = illustrative_control)
  }
}
tab(rows(sd_examples))

FLCI post-only att 0.015 1 -0.00392 0.20579 TRUE ok

The FLCI optimizes a linear estimator, accounting for its standard deviation and worst-case bias. C-LF adds a least-favorable first stage, calibrated by simulation, to the conditional test. The procedures need not give the same set or center; the table lists each piece of a set on its own row.

default_sd <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, M = .015, seed = 2026)
flci_sd <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, M = .015, method = "FLCI", seed = 2026)
tab(rows(list(default_SD = default_sd, FLCI_SD = flci_sd)))
example target M component lower upper success status
default_SD att 0.015 1 -0.01162 0.21349 TRUE ok
FLCI_SD att 0.015 1 0.01200 0.20705 TRUE ok

With method = NULL, the package uses C-LF for both SD and RM. For SD, full.path = NULL means FALSE for C-LF and Conditional and TRUE for the FLCI, so method = "FLCI" alone requests the full-path FLCI. The FLCI uses the pure pre-treatment second differences only under the full-path restriction, in addition to the last two pre-treatment periods that every post-only procedure extrapolates. Its coverage guarantee then no longer holds when those second differences exceed M, and its coverage also deteriorates when some cohorts contain only a few units.

5. Relative-magnitude restrictions

RM bounds each post-treatment change in a cohort’s block bias, |Δg,s−Δg,s−1||\Delta_{g,s}-\Delta_{g,s-1}|, by M‾\bar M times the same cohort’s largest absolute pre-treatment change; the bound has no units. The paper recommends choosing between RM and SD based on the empirical context. The cohort restriction is a union of cases, one for each combination of where and with which sign each cohort’s largest pre-treatment change occurs. In the minimum-wage application each positive bound requires 320 cases, and the examples therefore use the artificial panel.

With framework = "aggregate", RM restricts the aggregated coefficients using the aggregated path’s own pre-treatment benchmark, not a separate benchmark for each cohort.

rm_clf <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "RM", M = c(0, 1),
                             method = "C-LF", seed = 2026, control = illustrative_control)
rm_conditional <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "RM", M = c(0, 1),
                                     method = "Conditional", seed = 2026,
                                     control = illustrative_control)
rm_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "RM", M = c(0, 1),
                                   framework = "aggregate", seed = 2026,
                                   control = illustrative_control)
tab(rows(list(cohort_CLF = rm_clf, cohort_Conditional = rm_conditional,
              aggregate_CLF = rm_aggregate)))
example target M component lower upper success status
cohort_CLF att 0 1 0.02790 0.12001 TRUE ok
cohort_CLF att 1 1 -0.02910 0.18340 TRUE ok
cohort_Conditional att 0 1 0.02685 0.12107 TRUE ok
cohort_Conditional att 1 1 -0.02738 0.18158 TRUE ok
aggregate_CLF att 0 1 0.02637 0.11674 TRUE ok
aggregate_CLF att 1 1 -0.02350 0.16193 TRUE ok

RM has no full-path option and no FLCI; requesting either is an input error.

6. Read and reuse results

A cohort_fit holds the coefficients betahat, their full covariance Sigma, the bias map W, the normalization, the coefficient labels coordinate_info, the cohort masses, and sample diagnostics; coef() and vcov() extract the first two. A sensitivity result holds the conventional target estimates, every piece of each confidence set, the settings, and per-task diagnostics, including, for Conditional inference, the searched ranges that summary() tabulates.

Extracting confidence sets 

conditional <- sd_examples[["Conditional full path"]]

Each target and bound can occupy several rows of intervals, one for each piece. Keep the component column and every row when saving results; taking min(lower) and max(upper) would fill the gaps between pieces. results[[k]] follows the target order, then the sorted bounds.

f <- flci_sd$results[[1]]
tab(data.frame(conventional_estimate = flci_sd$estimates$estimate,
  optimized_center = mean(c(f$components$lower, f$components$upper)),
  standard_error = f$diagnostics$standard.error,
  maximum_bias = f$diagnostics$maximum.bias,
  half_length = f$diagnostics$half.length,
  solver_status = f$diagnostics$solver.status))
conventional_estimate optimized_center standard_error maximum_bias half_length solver_status
0.06147 0.10952 0.03969 0.03202 0.09753 direct_convergence_0

The FLCI’s linear weights (results[[k]]$weights) determine its optimized center, and the trade-off between its standard deviation and worst-case bias determines its half-length. flci_weights() tabulates the weights, and plot(result, type = "weights") draws them (FLCI weights).

Outcomes and statuses

Each target and bound ends in one of these outcomes:

Outcome Meaning How to recognize it
Nonempty set One or more computed pieces success = TRUE; bounds may be infinite
Certified empty set C-LF’s least-favorable first stage rejects every value success = TRUE, status empty, missing bounds
Unresolved empty search A finite search accepted no value and no certificate applies success = FALSE, status uncertified_empty_search, warning
Unsupported task No sampling variation in the target or tested moments, or too little pre-treatment history success = FALSE, a status such as unsupported_zero_variance or insufficient_prehistory, warning
Numerical failure or limit The search or solver failed or did not finish within its controls success = FALSE, a status such as evaluation_limit or inference_error, message, warning
Invalid input An argument or data requirement is violated Error; no inference is run

Read each row’s status and message rather than relying on a fixed list of status names. Further details are in these places:

Where What to check
result$intervals Every piece of each set, with bounds, center, plug-in bounds, success, status, and message
result$estimates, result$targets Conventional estimates and the cell weights that define each target
result$results[[k]] Detailed output for one target and bound, including procedure diagnostics and FLCI weights
result$settings The options used and the assigned task seeds
result$aggregation With balanced = TRUE under aggregate inference: the aggregation matrix, aggregated coefficients, covariance, and normalization on the balanced window
summary(result)$search.ranges The ranges a Conditional search covered
fit$diagnostics Cohort and cell counts, clusters, covariance rank, and flags for unbalanced designs, few clusters, single-cluster cells, extra rank loss, or near-zero post-treatment variance
fit$data_info$missingness Absent rows, missing outcomes, filled treatment statuses, and outcomes excluded by unknown leading statuses
fit$cluster_shares Under CR2, each cluster’s share of its cohort and the factor applied to its score

Before reporting a result, check its status, the sample support, the covariance diagnostics, and, for Conditional inference, the searched range. Then report the target and its weights, the cohort or aggregate representation, the restriction and the units of its bound, the procedure and SD scope, the confidence level, and every piece of the set.

7. Numerical controls and reproducibility

All numerical controls go in one uniquely named control list.

Key Default Meaning
lf.sims 2000 C-LF calibration draws (not bootstrap replications)
grid.points 101 Grid points, at least 5; for Conditional searches with grid.radius above 8, the reference density
endpoint.tol NULL Endpoint tolerance in outcome units; by default 1e-5 times the conventional target standard error
grid.radius 8 Initial search margin for Conditional and RM C-LF (see ?cohort_sensitivity); not used by SD C-LF
max.expansions 6 Range doublings for Conditional, including the two expansions needed to confirm a stable range (0 or 1 returns no set), and range expansions for RM C-LF; not used by SD C-LF
max.refinements 3 Finer-grid retries after an unresolved search; 0 disables them
max.evaluations 100000 Point evaluations per target and bound, counted across all probes, audits, and retries
topology.audit TRUE FALSE skips the interior grid comparisons; domain and endpoint checks remain
max.components 100000 Maximum number of RM cases
flci.solver "direct" FLCI optimizer, "direct" or "nested" (requires CVXR)
flci.control list() Solver-specific settings, listed below

More calibration draws reduce the Monte Carlo noise in C-LF, and a denser grid adds point tests; both take more time. For final results, increase the calibration draws and check the numerical diagnostics.

Conditional and C-LF sets come from a finite numerical search. A Conditional search does not rule out pieces outside the range it searched, which summary(result)$search.ranges reports. For SD, C-LF searches a range that its first stage certifies (if it cannot certify one, it reports no set), but this certifies only the outer range, not the interior. Any finite grid can miss very narrow pieces or gaps. The evaluation count does not limit running time.

limited <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, M = .015, method = "Conditional", seed = 2026,
  control = list(grid.points = 21L, max.evaluations = 10L))
#> Warning: 1 inference task(s) failed; inspect intervals$status and
#> intervals$message.
tab(limited$intervals[, c("status", "message")])
status message
evaluation_limit The requested wider Conditional grid exceeds the cumulative point-evaluation budget or R’s integer range.

The warning and failed status mark a computational limit: the calculation stopped before it resolved the set, so the result is neither an empty confidence set nor a rejection.

With an explicit seed, each task receives a fixed random-number stream, the results do not depend on the number of workers, and the caller’s random-number state is restored; seed = NULL draws the task seeds from the caller’s stream. parallel = TRUE runs independent target and bound tasks, or the cases of a single RM task, on cores workers.

FLCI solvers

Solver flci.control key Default and constraint
direct n_random_starts 8L, nonnegative integer
direct maxit 20000L, nonnegative integer
nested solver "ECOS", one available CVXR solver name
nested solver_opts list(), named options passed to CVXR
nested outer_tol 1e-7, positive
nested grid_size 15L, integer at least 3
nested feasibility_tol 1e-6, positive
nested objective_tol 1e-6, positive

Each key belongs to its solver, and the two lists cannot be mixed.

8. Supply external estimates and construct W

External input needs the full named vector of cohort-period coefficients β̂\hat\beta (pre-treatment, reference, and post-treatment), its joint covariance Σ\Sigma, an invertible bias map WW with δ=WΔ\delta=W\Delta, and deterministic normalization constraints NN with Nβ̂=0N\hat\beta=0 and NΣ=0N\Sigma=0; WW must preserve the normalization. The covariance may be singular (positive semidefinite), as normalizations usually make it. The pre-treatment coefficients must be block-bias estimates as defined in the paper. Marginal standard errors, an aggregated event study, or residual pre-trends do not carry this information.

The round trip below passes the artificial fit’s estimates through cohort_input() and reruns the default analysis.

external <- cohort_input(betahat = coef(small_fit), vcov = vcov(small_fit),
  coefficient_info = small_fit$coordinate_info, W = small_fit$W,
  normalization = small_fit$normalization,
  cohort_sizes = small_fit$cohort_masses, estimator = "imp")
external_result <- cohort_sensitivity(external, M = .015, seed = 2026)
tab(rows(list(internal = default_sd, external = external_result)))
example target M component lower upper success status
internal att 0.015 1 -0.01162 0.21349 TRUE ok
external att 0.015 1 -0.01162 0.21349 TRUE ok

coefficient_info needs the columns coordinate, integer cohort, integer relative_period, and type ("pre" for pre-treatment and reference coefficients, "post" otherwise). betahat must be named; the covariance and W need row and column names, and the normalization needs column names, that match the coefficient labels, and cohort_input() aligns them. cohort_sizes needs one positive finite value per treated cohort, named by its adoption index.

W describes a mapping, not an estimator 

W_nyt <- build_W(cohort_times = c(3, 4), cohort_sizes = c(`3` = 24, `4` = 24),
                 never_treated_size = 24, n_periods = 4, estimator = "cs_nyt")
dim(W_nyt)
#> [1] 8 8
W_nyt[grepl("delta_post", rownames(W_nyt)), , drop = FALSE]

#> delta_post_g3_s1                0               0                0
#> delta_post_g3_s2                0               0                0
#> delta_post_g4_s1                0               0                0
#>                  delta_pre_g4_s-1 delta_pre_g4_s0 delta_post_g3_s1
#> delta_post_g3_s1              0.0               0                1
#> delta_post_g3_s2             -0.5               0                0
#> delta_post_g4_s1              0.0               0                0
#>                  delta_post_g3_s2 delta_post_g4_s1
#> delta_post_g3_s1                0              0.0
#> delta_post_g3_s2                1              0.5
#> delta_post_g4_s1                0              1.0

build_W() constructs the bias map for a balanced design with fixed cohort sizes; it does not estimate coefficients or covariances. cohort_times are distinct integer adoption indices from 2 to n_periods, and all sizes, including the never-treated size, must be positive.

Too little pre-treatment history

A fit can have too little pre-treatment history for sensitivity analysis:

short_history <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = subset(small, time >= 2),
                            index = c("id", "time"), estimator = "cs_nt")
short_result <- cohort_sensitivity(short_history, M = .015, seed = 2026)
#> Warning: 1 inference task(s) failed; inspect intervals$status and
#> intervals$message.
tab(sets(short_result))
target M component lower upper success status
att 0.015 1 NA NA FALSE insufficient_prehistory 
tab(short_result$intervals[, c("status", "message")])
status message
insufficient_prehistory Sensitivity analysis requires at least two pre-treatment periods for every included cohort/path.

Under cohort inference, every treated cohort needs at least two pre-treatment periods; this task returns insufficient_prehistory and no set. One post-treatment period is enough, as for the period-4 cohort of the full artificial panel.

9. Plot choices

Fit plots accept type = "dynamic" (the default) or "cohort-dynamic"; sensitivity plots take their form from the computed target. main, xlab, and ylab set the labels, and color overrides the framework color. All plots return ggplot objects, which accept further ggplot2 layers.

plot(fit_imp, type = "cohort-dynamic", cohorts = chosen_cohort,
  main = "Conventional coefficients for one cohort",
  xlab = "Relative period", ylab = "Log teen employment")

plot(att, M = c(0, .015, .02), identified.set = FALSE,
  main = "Selected minimum-wage bounds",
  xlab = "Allowed curvature M", ylab = "Log teen employment", color = "#5A3E85") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

identified.set = FALSE removes the plug-in band from ATT plots without changing the confidence sets. paper_palette() returns the package’s colors for representations, procedures, or cohorts.

For FLCI results, plot(result, type = "weights") draws the weights as a heatmap instead of the sets; weights, by, targets, and labels choose what it shows (FLCI weights).
